instruction.what: Step 3.1, the elements of one subgroup (stage 4, C1; the end of the loop for the subgroup): what the evidence of the subgroup shows of the elements of a behaviour of the inner being. The input is the evidence observations of the subgroup by marker (`to_take_up`, the senses first, then the 2.1 findings and the older evidence), not the verses; the verses are kept for an occasional read-back. A finding is a building block, never a claim about the behaviour as a whole (that is stage 5).
read: Read the observations to take up, in order: the senses (1.1) and their enrichments (1.2) first, then the 2.1 findings (pairings, qualifiers, entities, direction, double meanings), then the older evidence. The inner-being workings work more with the senses than with the surfaces, so findings rest on the senses first.

For each item a finding may use (`uses`): what is done and its mode (operation, with its chain), whether a refusal or a pursuit (polarity), what it is directed at (object), the outward act (enactment), the other party with the route (party), the circumstance, and what a qualifier or a variation of the word gives the working (role, the dimension). Never the meaning of the word (stage 1).

Read the older inner-being observations (`older_inner_being`) with them: each is considered first, accepted with a trace to evidence, restated where it says more than the evidence, consumed where a finding says the same, merged, or deleted where it cannot be made true.
Go back to a verse (`verses`) only where the evidence does not settle the question, and say why.
write: Fill `answer.findings`: each one observation, with a `key` unique in the answer, `kind` (of the item's kinds), `text`, `basis` (stated or read), `parts` with `item` (one of `uses`) and what the item needs (with `grounds`), and `nodes`: a `traced` node on each observation it rests on (from `to_take_up` or `may_rest_on_besides`) and an `occurrence` node, with its `role` chosen from the verse (characteristic, qualifier, object, relational target, enactment or standalone), on the occurrences those observations cover.
An occurrence outside the observations a finding rests on is allowed only with a `read_back` entry on the finding: {verse: the osis id, why}.
`not_used`: {observation id: reason} for every observation to take up that no finding rests on. Every one is rested on or declared, never both.

`older`: answer, once, each older inner-being observation (`older_inner_being`) that has a node on an occurrence your findings name (RW-13; the record lists any it misses, and refuses an answer to one on no named occurrence: those are shown, not demanded, IB-05): keep (with nature inner_being: it stands, traced to evidence), restate, merge, consume (carriers ["this"] or ids, mapping), delete_neither, or defer (collection, nature, finding).
`existing`: answer every earlier reading (`earlier_readings`: inner being of an earlier grouping on these occurrences) with accept, modify, delete, merge or leave, and its reason.
The text says what the evidence shows of the element; it names its verses; it never restates a verse and never states the behaviour as a whole.

In place of writing `nodes`, a finding may name `rests_on` (the observations it rests on) and `role` (the node role of the words they cover; `roles` {occurrence: role, or "" to leave one out} for the exceptions): the recorder writes a traced node on each and an occurrence node on each occurrence they cover (each observation's `covers` or `occurrences` lists them). Nodes written by hand are kept.

Then: Collection-Build.ps1 -Action CheckAnswer -File <the answer file>: every problem at once, each with its rule, nothing written; correct the answer until it finds none, then -Action RecordElements -File <the answer file>. The record refuses the whole file on any fault and lists every fault.

keep.text: Stage 4 starts from the observations, not the verses (researcher, #2526 Q7, 2026-11-21): the subgroups and the stage 3 observations on them are the input, the behaviours are discovered from analysing them, and the base data is read back into only occasionally. Every finding of step 3.1 or 3.2 rests on named observations (a traced node on each, with an occurrence node as well) and its occurrence nodes lie within the occurrences those observations cover; an occurrence outside them is allowed only where the finding records a read-back (the verse and why). Each node has a role from reading.node_roles other than lexical, chosen by the reading. A 3.3 finding carries nodes on the occurrences of both sides in the shared verses. In 3.1 a qualification finding may also hold, with the role qualifier, the occurrences of the partner words the subgroup's 2.1 qualifier observations name, where the reading judges the qualifier bears on the working; a qualifier that does not bear on it is declared in not_used with its reason, never forced into a finding.

A finding of a stage 4 row is checked by the rules of observationrecord.check and check_item_parts (kind, text, basis, route, parts.item and what the item needs, node roles, collection of each node) and by RG, RW and RS, which are not restated here: one observation for each finding, never a duplicate, with a node on each word it applies to (RO11, RW-03); founded in the observations and never a restatement of the verse (B:131); parts.item is one of the items the row's item uses (cfg_setting layer.reading). An observation whose nodes all bear on an act is refused: those words are nodes of the observation of the act. A finding is a building block of a behaviour and never a claim (stage 5).

Nothing the step reads is lost on the way to stage 5. Step 3.1: every stage 3 observation of the subgroup is rested on by a finding or declared in not_used with its reason in words. Step 3.2: every 3.1 observation of the collection is gathered into a behaviour (a traced node on it from a flag finding of type discovery) or declared in not_gathered with its reason, and the row has at least one behaviour unless it is recorded as none with its reason. A behaviour names and gathers; it makes no claim about what the behaviour is.

An earlier inner-being observation with a node on the occurrences of a 3.1 row (any stage but those of the build: lexical, layer-1, layer-2, layer-3.1 to layer-3.3, and layer-3 before 2026-11-26) is shown in the pull for information and may be actioned in `existing`: accepted, modified, deleted, merged or left, each with its reason, through observationrecord (RW-01, RW-09); nothing is demanded of it, and it counts for nothing in the check. A row answered again withdraws its earlier observations with the reason. Every older live observation with a node on an occurrence of the row is answered in fill.older at the record of the row (RW-13); this rule's `existing` actions of stage 4 are unchanged.

Every live observation marked inner_being holds at least one live traced node on a live observation marked evidence, or on a live inner-being observation that itself traces to evidence (the trace chain of stage 4: a 3.2 behaviour traces the 3.1 elements it gathers, a 3.3 match the 3.1 and 3.2 observations it comes from; at most three links), unless it is recorded self-evidencing: it quotes its verse in full and holds a word node for every word it relies on. A traced node never points at a deleted observation. A trace points first at existing evidence; an evidence observation is created only when none states the fact and it states what the nodes and the quotation do not. An inner-being observation traced to evidence not yet marked is pending, not failed.

Find the main inner-being operation, and give every word that bears on it its role in this finding (cfg_setting reading.node_roles): characteristic, qualifier and what it gives the characteristic, object or content, relational target, or enactment. A word read in the verse that holds nothing for the inner being is standalone. The role comes from this verse, never from the cluster tag. Where a standalone word proves to qualify a characteristic, it is a qualifier of it.

A qualifier gets no separate account of itself, but what it gives the characteristic it binds to is evaluated for its value and recorded as a qualification finding, applied by its nodes to the qualifier (role qualifier) and the characteristic (role characteristic). What it gives can vary widely: grade, nature, impact, size, relation, a measure, strengthening, ground, cause, object, setting or bait are examples, not a list (#2273 D9). A qualifier whose usage varies across contexts may earn its own reading later.

Record the parties: who bears the act, who causes it, who is acted on (source, target, impact, purpose), and the route (cfg_enum observation_route), whose meaning is cfg_behaviour_rule 72 (route-verses-hib-other-beings-data-only): A another being in its own right, B another being with the human inner being, C no bearing, data only; a verse may take A and B. A non-human being is never itself a HIB; a collective stays one HIB; an implied party is named as referential, never asserted.
Never close a verse or item on 'not X'. A role label is never a verdict; the close records what the verse is. Silence about the inner being is a finding, recorded as data with its reason.
A phenomenon hidden behind a stated or refrained act may be named, with the verb, clause or stated silence that grounds it, and whether it is stated or read.
Keep the source of an interior state apart from the source of an enablement to act.

A tagged word that works adverbially in an occurrence (a noun with a preposition qualifying the predicate, as 'in the counsel of the wicked') is a qualifier there, not the verse's characteristic. The role is per occurrence: the same word may be the characteristic elsewhere.
In a simile, the predicates of the vehicle (the tree that yields, does not wither) are read for what they say of the one compared (the tenor), not as the vehicle's own acts.
One observation per finding, never a duplicate description; a finding applying to several verses or words carries several nodes, each with the word's role in it.
One observation per finding: the same description is never written twice. Applied to another verse, word or scope it gains a node on the existing observation.
Observation text is concise and tied to this verse's content, never a restatement of the word's dictionary sense. A transliteration is never given without its gloss.

An observation is created with its marker (ib_observation.nature, from the item answered, cfg_setting layer.reading items.<item>.nature; a finding file never sets it) and every word node with the columns of layer.reading node_required. A column the data cannot give (layer.reading node_gap_columns: an empty morph in the source row, a surface with no placement in the collection index) is left empty and its reason is kept on the node (disposition_note); any other missing column refuses the whole file and nothing is written. A trace to a deleted observation is refused (IB-07).

Evidence states what the data are or show, tied to a verse. Inner being states how something works in the inner being, based on evidence, a building block of the stage 5 claims. The marker (ib_observation.nature) follows the content and purpose of the observation, never its stage (RS-04): an observation of any stage may be inner being when it traces to evidence. One that states both is split. The marker is set when the observation is created, by the item that is answered (cfg_setting layer.reading items.<item>.nature); a finding file never sets it; the validation changes it only where the content shows the item's nature does not hold.

The study's primary focus is the human inner being (HIB). Each verse read is routed by what it shows, and the route is recorded in its observation. (A) Other beings in their own right: a word used of God, angels, other spirits or nature (non-HIB) is routed to Ch 13 "Other beings" (13.1 Divine, 13.2 Angels, 13.3 Other spirits, 13.4 Nature), read for what the verses say that being is and does; for God, also how his character passed to the HIB through creation in his image, held open (#1984). (B) Another being interacting with the HIB is fully in HIB scope. A verse may take A and B, described from different angles. (C) A verse with no inner-being and no other-being bearing is still assessed and recorded as data, and does not enter the narrative.

A node is on one occurrence (verse_lexical_id) and carries the collection of its surface (a supportive node, the collection of the surface it supports); a node already on the observation for the same occurrence is not written twice, and takes the role. A node with no collection to carry, or on a verse out of scope (B:130), is not written and is listed.

LayerCheck validates a stage 4 row from the tables alone: the demanded occurrences and the observations the row may rest on are re-derived; at least one live observation of the stage of its step (layer-3.1, layer-3.2 or layer-3.3) with its stable_key on the row; each observation's parts still valid and its item one the row uses; each live node has a valid role, a collection and its subgroup; each observation has a traced node on an observation the row may rest on; in 3.1 and 3.2 each occurrence node lies in the occurrences of the observations it rests on or its verse is in the recorded read-back; the completeness of IB-04 (not_used, not_gathered, the behaviour of 3.2); no observation restates a run of the verse longer than reading.observation_items max_verse_words_copied. A row that fails is unvalidated and its step is not closed.

A behaviour (step 3.2) is one working of the inner being: one core operation, who or what does what, shown by several element observations of 3.1. Elements that show the same operation belong to one behaviour, whatever their mode, polarity, object, party or circumstance, and in whatever subgroup they sit; those differences are written as relating findings (operation, chain, party, circumstance, role). Different operations linked in sequence are a chain between behaviours, not one behaviour. A group that holds two operations is split; two groups that hold one operation are joined. An element that shows no working of a human inner being (another being in its own right, route A of B:72; a word that is not an act of the mind) is declared not gathered with its reason. A behaviour is named by what is done, never by what it means for the inner being (stage 5).

A step of the layered reading opens only when the grouping is finished (every surface placed in a subgroup or isolated with its reason, every subgroup holding a surface) and the previous step is closed; with -Subgroup the needs and gates are judged for that subgroup alone (#2538). Step S1 is read after the grouping; step 1.1 needs step S1 closed: every word of the subgroup (surface and lettered Strong's code) answered and validated. Opening derives one ledger row for each aspect the data demands (cfg_setting layer.reading); an aspect the data no longer demands is retired, a new one is added, and a second open changes nothing.

The nodes of a layer observation are the occurrences the aspect demands (a word's occurrences, the group's occurrences, the partner's occurrences in the verses they share), written by the recorder with the collection and the subgroup of each surface; they are never typed. An item answered by senses (word-sense) names, for each sense, the occurrences it holds for, and together the senses cover every occurrence; the recorder checks them against the data. The interpretation is the observation text, founded in what the evidence shows (basis stated or read, B:131) and tied to its verses (the text names them and does not restate them): the items of every step (S1, 1.1, 1.2, 2.1) state what the dictionary, the verses and the stored structure show of a word and never what a word does for the inner being; their nodes carry the role lexical and no route. The whole file is checked and written in one transaction; any problem refuses all of it. A row answered again withdraws its earlier observations with the reason.

An aspect is recorded as none only where its item allows it (cfg_setting layer.reading none_allowed) and with its reason in words. A group definition and a group's Strong's enrichment are always observed.

A read or record command names a live collection, a live subgroup of it where the read is by subgroup, and a step or item the layered reading knows. A command that names one that does not exist is refused and writes nothing.

An answer is the output form its read wrote: the `command` of that read; every entry an object, or a list, where the form has one; each field in its place with its type (a key unique in the answer, a text, a reason in words); each item answered once; and at least one entry where the form asks for entries. A file in another shape is refused whole and nothing is written.

Every ledger row, occurrence, observation, sense, node, verse and collection an answer names is one the packet offered for this unit, or a key the answer itself defines, and is live in the database. A name outside them is refused.

Every coded value of an answer (kind, basis, item, part, role, route, mode, polarity, flag type, disposition, verdict, action, nature, stage, status) is one of the values the configuration allows for it (cfg_enum, cfg_setting layer.reading, reading.observation_items, validate.reading), as the packet lists them. Any other value is refused.

A read or record runs only where the ledger has its unit at that step: the row open, or answered and not yet validated, and the steps before it closed (S1 before 1.1; the 2.1 rows before the sweep; the sweep before the evidence validation; its gate before 3.1; every subgroup through 3.1 before 3.2). Out of order it is refused, and the message names what comes first.

A read writes its packet within the time and size the configuration sets (cfg_setting layer.read_types: limits, package_max_chars, read_max_seconds). A read that would exceed them is refused, nothing is written, and the limit is named.

The code of the reading runs only where the configuration it reads is in place (the settings, steps, items, natures, enums and rules it names). Where the code is ahead of the configuration, the command is refused and names what is missing.

When a verse is worked, every existing observation and node on it, of any stage, is checked against the verse by its wording. The stage is not an indication of the nature of an observation and is never used to filter. Each observation is accepted, modified (changed in place; the old value, the new value and the reason are kept in ib_observation_change), soft deleted (the `deleted` column, with the reason), merged (a duplicate description, into the observation that is kept) or, when its wording shows it is not verse understanding, left exactly as it is with the reason. The check's fixes are part of it and need no separate approval. Nothing is physically deleted.
No observation is changed except by a reading, and every change is recorded with its reason. An observation no longer supported by the verse is soft-deleted, with the reason.

Every older live observation with a live node on an occurrence of the row (a stage that is not the build's own) is answered in fill.older when the row is recorded, once: keep or restate (each with its marker), merge into a named observation, consume (live observations carry its meaning, stated in words, verified before it is deleted), delete as neither (comment first), or defer to a named collection (marked now; only the finding is left to that collection). An observation already marked by the validation, answered in a build or deferred is not asked again. A new observation whose text equals that of another live observation of the collection is refused, the other named. LayerCheck re-derives both from the tables. The end state of a collection's build is that every observation of its scope is marked and fixed or deleted, every word node complete or with its reason, and each deferral owned by a named collection.

A lookup of related data in the build or the validation is by an indexed column and takes a chunk of ids (cfg_setting layer.scan chunk); none runs once for each item of a list, and a statement that uses more work than layer.scan max_vm_ops is stopped and named, nothing written (lib/scanguard.py). The tests refuse a statement of the build whose query plan scans a table (layer.scan scan_ok lists the temporary tables a statement may scan).

An older observation is deleted as consumed only when live observations carry its meaning: every word occurrence of it is on a live node of a carrier or named as not carried with its reason, the mapping is stated in words (what the old says, which carrier states each part), the traces to it are re-pointed or replaced, and the consumption is kept as `consumed_by`. An observation that holds more than one finding is split first.

An observation that is neither evidence nor inner being contributes nothing to the purposes of the observations (researcher, 2026-11-22): it is commented with its reason and the word occurrences no other live observation holds, then deleted. An observation already marked, or one another observation traces, is not deleted this way.

to_take_up.text: Chasing to overtake: running after a person, band or army to overtake, capture or strike them, in Gen 14:15, Exo 14:9, Jos 10:19, Judg 4:16, Judg 20:45, Num 14:45, 1Sa 30:8, 2Sa 2:19, 2Ki 25:5 and the many other battle and flight narratives.

Hounding to destroy: pursuit aimed at a person's life, standing or the weak, driven in some verses by desire or anger, in Exo 15:9, Deu 19:6, 1Sa 25:29, Psa 7:5, Psa 71:11, Psa 109:16, Psa 143:3, Job 19:22, Amo 1:11, Lam 3:43 and Rev 12:13.

Pursuit by God or by what is not a person: God pursuing with tempest, sword or flood (Psa 83:15, Jer 29:18, Lam 3:66, Nah 1:8, Job 13:25), and curses, diseases, blood and the sword as pursuers (Deu 28:22, Deu 28:45, Eze 35:6, Jer 48:2), with honor chased off in Job 30:15.
Pursuit of a good: going after righteousness, peace, love and the virtues as an aim, in Rom 9:30, Rom 9:31, Rom 14:19, 1Cor 14:1, 1Ti 6:11, 2Ti 2:22, 1Pe 3:11, Psa 34:14 and Isa 51:1.
Going after a forbidden desire: the cities of Jude 7 going after other flesh, and the wife of Hos 2:7 chasing her lovers without reaching them.

radaph (H7291) is to be behind and follow after, to chase and put to flight; achar (H0310A, after) marks the one chased as ahead; dabaq (H1692) adds keeping close and overtaking in Judg 20:45, and katat (H3807, to crush) in Num 14:45 adds the beating down the ESV renders as pursuit. The lexicon bears out the chase.

radaph (H7291) has the figurative sense to persecute and harass, and dioko (G1377) the sense to oppress a person or group systematically, the dragon's pursuit in Rev 12:13; al (H5921A, upon) in Amo 1:11 is a preposition and adds no meaning. The lexicon bears out a hostile pursuit.

radaph (H7291) carries no sense of its own for a pursuer that is God, a curse or blood; the lexicon gives the chase, and the verses Psa 83:15, Deu 28:45 and Eze 35:6 supply the pursuer. halak (H1980N) with achar in Jer 48:2 is to go after, given here to the sword.

dioko (G1377) from the image of the chase has the sense of pressing on to a goal and following eagerly to acquire it, which Rom 14:19 and 1Ti 6:11 use; radaph (H7291) has the figurative sense to follow after and aim to secure, used in Psa 34:14 and Isa 51:1. de (G1161) is a particle and adds no meaning.

aperchomai (G0565) is to go away or depart, and opiso (G3694, after) in Jude 7 turns the going away into a going after; radaph (H7291) in Hos 2:7 is the chase itself. The lexicon has no sense of desire in these codes; the desire is in the objects the verses name.

In Gen 35:5, Exo 14:4, Deu 19:6, Jos 8:16, Jos 10:19, 2Sa 17:1, 2Sa 20:6, 2Sa 20:7 and 2Sa 20:13 the surface pursue stands on two codes at one place, radaph (H7291) and achar (H0310A, after): the verb and the word that marks the one chased as ahead.

In the other Hebrew verses of the row, among them Exo 15:9, Deu 28:45, Psa 34:14, Lam 3:66, Hos 2:7 and Nah 1:8, the surface pursue stands on radaph (H7291) alone, whether the object is a person, a good or the one God pursues.
In Jer 48:2 the surface pursue stands on halak (H1980N, go) with achar (H0310A, after), not on radaph: the sword goes after Madmen.
In Rom 9:30, Rom 14:19, 1Cor 14:1, 1Ti 6:11, 2Ti 2:22 and 1Pe 3:11 the surface pursue stands on dioko (G1377), and in 1Ti 6:11 also on de (G1161, but), the particle at the same place.

In Exo 14:8, Exo 14:9, Jos 8:16, Judg 4:16, 2Sa 2:19, 2Ki 9:27, Jer 39:5 and the other verses where both stand, the surface pursued holds radaph (H7291) and achar (H0310A, after) at one place, the verb with the word that sets the one chased ahead.
In Amo 1:11 the surface pursued holds radaph (H7291) with al (H5921A, upon), so the brother Edom pursued stands as the one the pursuit comes upon.
In Gen 14:15, Exo 14:23, Jos 8:24, 1Sa 30:10, Psa 18:37, Psa 109:16, Job 30:15 and the other verses of radaph alone, the surface pursued stands on radaph (H7291) with no second code.
In Num 14:45 the surface pursued stands on katat (H3807, crush) and in Judg 20:45 on dabaq (H1692, keep close): neither is radaph, and the English gives both as pursuit.
In Rom 9:31 and Rev 12:13 the surface pursued stands on dioko (G1377), and in Jude 7 on aperchomai (G0565, go away) with opiso (G3694, after), a going away after unnatural desire.

In Gen 31:23, Exo 14:23, Jos 2:7, Jos 8:16, Jos 8:17, Judg 7:23, 1Sa 24:14, 2Sa 2:19, 2Sa 20:7 and the other verses where it stands, achar (H0310A, after, behind) follows the verb of pursuit and points to the one chased; it gives direction, not a grade.
In Gen 35:5, 2Sa 2:28 and Rom 9:30 the negator reaches the pursuit itself: the cities did not pursue, Joab's men pursued Israel no more, and the nations did not pursue righteousness.

In Hos 2:7 and Rom 9:31 the negator reaches the outcome of the pursuit: the lovers are not overtaken or found, and Israel did not reach the law it pursued; in Hos 2:7 first, better, now and then belong to her turning back.

In 2Sa 2:19, 2Sa 22:38, Psa 18:37, Lam 3:43 and Amo 1:11 the qualifier tells how the pursuit was carried on: not turning aside or back, without pity, and in Amo 1:11 with anger kept perpetually and forever, whose punishment is not revoked.

In Psa 109:16 and Eze 35:6 a negated clause gives the reason for the pursuit or its punishment: he did not remember to show kindness, and you did not hate bloodshed; Eze 35:6 opens with an oath and 'therefore'.
In Psa 109:16, Job 13:25, Jude 7 and Rev 12:13 the qualifier falls on what is pursued: the poor and needy, dry chaff, desire that is unnatural, and the woman who bore the male child.

In Psa 34:14, 1Pe 3:11, 2Ti 2:22 and Hos 8:3 evil and good, youthful and pure set the pursuit against what is turned from or fled: turning from evil and doing good, fleeing youthful passions with those of a pure heart, and the good Israel spurned.

In the other verses of the row, among them Gen 31:23, Deu 19:6, Jos 10:19, 1Sa 25:29, 2Sa 20:6, 2Ki 9:27, Jer 48:2 and 1Cor 14:1, the negators, adverbs and adjectives reach other words of the verse, a length of days, a place, a time, a second clause, and not the pursuit.

In the battle and flight narratives (Gen 14:15, Jos 8:16, Judg 4:16, Judg 7:25, 1Sa 23:25, 2Sa 2:19, 2Sa 20:10, 2Ki 9:27, Jer 39:5 and the rest) both pursuer and pursued are named persons, peoples or bands: Pharaoh, Barak, David, Saul, Abner, Joab, Sheba, Jehu, Zedekiah, the men of Israel; in Rev 12:13 the one pursued is the woman.

God is named in many of the verses: as the one who pursues (Lam 3:66, Eze 35:6), who hardens Pharaoh's heart or sends terror (Exo 14:4, Gen 35:5), who is asked or gives the enemy over (1Sa 30:8, Jos 10:19), in whose likeness the friends pursue (Job 19:22), and as the Lord sought or called on (Isa 51:1, 2Ti 2:22).
In Lam 3:66, Eze 35:6, Deu 28:22 and Deu 28:45 the pursuit runs from God, or from what he sends (diseases, curses, blood), toward a people or an enemy, to destroy or overtake them.

In Isa 51:1, 1Ti 6:11 and 2Ti 2:22 the pursuit runs from a person toward a good, righteousness and the virtues, with the Lord named as the one sought or called on, and in 1Ti 6:11 and 2Ti 2:22 away from what is fled.
In 1Sa 25:29, Psa 71:11 and Job 19:22 the pursuit runs from enemies or friends toward a person's life, and God is named on the side of the one pursued or as the likeness of the pursuers.

In the battle and flight narratives (Gen 14:15, Exo 14:9, Jos 8:16, Judg 4:16, 1Sa 23:25, 2Sa 2:19, 2Ki 9:27, Jer 39:5 and the rest) and in Amo 1:11 and Rev 12:13 the pursuit runs from one person or force toward another who flees, ahead of the pursuer.
In Psa 143:3 'crushed' (H1792) follows the pursuit of the speaker's soul: the enemy who pursued has crushed his life to the ground.
In Deu 19:6 'anger' (lev, H3824, the heart that is hot) is the state in which the avenger of blood pursues the manslayer, the reason the law gives for the cities of refuge.
In Lam 3:43 and Lam 3:66 'anger' (af, H0639G) is God's: he wrapped himself in anger and pursued Zion, and is asked to pursue the enemies in anger.
In Amo 1:11 'anger' (H0639G) and 'wrath' (H5678) are Edom's toward his brother, torn and kept forever, beside the pursuit with the sword.
In 1Sa 30:8 'inquired' (H7592 with H0559) comes before the pursuit: David asks the Lord whether to pursue, and the answer commands it.
In Rom 9:30 'faith' (pistis, G4102G) names the righteousness the nations reached without pursuing it, a righteousness by faith.
In 1Ti 6:11 and 2Ti 2:22 'faith' (G4102G) is one of the goods named as objects of the command to pursue, beside righteousness and love.
In Eze 35:6 'prepare' (H6213H) is God's act that comes before the pursuit: he prepares Edom for blood, and then blood pursues.
In Jos 8:16 and Judg 7:23 'called' (H2199, H6817) is the summoning of the people, which comes before and sets off the pursuit.
In 2Ti 2:22 'call on' (G1941) names the company in which the pursuit is made: people who call on the Lord with a heart that is pure.
In Jer 29:18 'reproach' (H2781) is among what the people become among the nations after God pursues them with sword, famine and pestilence.
In 2Sa 17:1 'choose' (H0977) is Ahithophel's selecting of twelve thousand men, the first step of the pursuit he proposes against David.
In 2Sa 24:13 'decide' (H7200J) is put to David among three judgments, one of them fleeing while foes pursue.
In 2Ti 2:22 'pure' (G2513) qualifies the heart of those with whom the pursuit is to be made.
In 2Sa 2:28 'fight' (H3898A with H5750) is stopped together with the pursuit at the trumpet: they pursued no more and fought no more.
In Deu 28:45 'commanded' (H6680) belongs to the commandments not kept, the reason the curses pursue and overtake.
In Psa 109:16, Lam 3:43 and Amo 1:11 kindness or pity (H2617A, H2550, H7356B) is withheld from the one pursued: no kindness remembered, killing without pity, pity cast off.
In 1Ti 6:11 'gentleness' (G4239) is the last of the goods the man of God is told to pursue.
In Job 13:25 'driven' (H5086) describes the leaf, and in Jer 29:18 'driven' (H5080 with H0834A) names the nations where God has scattered the people he pursues.
In Jer 39:5 'sentence' (H4941G with H0854) is passed on Zedekiah after he was pursued and overtaken.
In Jude 7 'eternal' (G0166) qualifies the fire of the punishment that follows going after unnatural desire.
In Deu 28:45 'obey' (H8085H) is negated: not obeying the voice of the Lord is the reason the curses pursue.
In Deu 28:22 'strike' (H5221) is the Lord's striking with disease, the things that then pursue until they perish.
In Exo 15:9 'desire' (nephesh, H5315L) is the enemy's, which is to have its fill of them: it stands in the same boast as I will pursue and overtake.
In 1Cor 14:1 'earnestly desire' (zeloo, G2206) is the second command after 'Pursue love', with the spiritual gifts as its object.
In 2Ti 2:22 'passions' (G1939) are the youthful ones to be fled, set against what is to be pursued.
In Jude 7 'desire' (sarx, G4561, flesh) is what the cities went after, flesh that is other, rendered unnatural desire.

In Exo 15:9, Deu 28:45, 2Sa 22:38, Psa 18:37 and Lam 3:66 destroying or consuming (H3423H, H8045, H3615H) is the end the pursuit aims at or reaches: the pursuer does not turn back until the pursued are consumed.
In Deu 11:4 'destroyed' (H0006) falls on the pursuers: the Egyptians who pursued Israel were destroyed by the Lord at the Red Sea.
In Deu 19:6, 2Sa 20:10, 2Ki 9:27 and Psa 109:16 death (H4194, H4191) is what the pursuit brings or aims at: the manslayer struck fatally, Amasa and Ahaziah dead, the needy pursued to be put to death.
In Deu 28:22 'perish' (H0006) is the end set for the pursuit of the diseases: they pursue until the people perish.
In Job 13:25 'dry' (H3002) qualifies the chaff Job asks whether God will pursue, a thing too light to be worth the chase.
In Jos 10:19 'stay' (H5975G) is negated: the men are not to stand still but to pursue the enemy.

In Judg 1:6, Judg 8:12, Judg 20:45, 2Sa 20:6, 2Sa 24:13, 1Ki 20:20 and 2Ki 9:27 fleeing or escaping (H5127, H4422, H5337) is what the pursued do, the other half of the chase, and in 1Ki 20:20 Ben-hadad escapes.
In 1Ti 6:11 and 2Ti 2:22 'flee' (pheugo, G5343) is commanded together with pursue: the man of God flees these things, or youthful passions, and pursues righteousness.
In Psa 34:14 and 1Pe 3:11 'evil' (H7451B, G2556G) is what one turns away from before seeking peace and pursuing it.
In 1Sa 26:18 'evil' (H7451I) is denied by David: he asks what evil is on his hands that Saul pursues him.
In 1Sa 30:10 'exhausted' (H6296) describes the two hundred who stayed behind at the brook Besor, while David pursued with four hundred.
In Gen 35:5 'terror' (H2847) from God falls on the surrounding cities, and the verse gives it as the reason no pursuit of Jacob's sons was made.

In Judg 8:12, Psa 83:15 and Jer 29:18 panic, terror or horror (H2729, H0926, H2189, H8047H) goes with the pursuit: Gideon throws the army into a panic, God is asked to terrify with his hurricane, and the pursued are made a horror.
In Job 13:25 and Job 30:15 frightening and terrors (H6206, H1091 with H5921A) are on the side of the one pursued: a leaf frightened, terrors turned on Job.
In Psa 109:16 'remember' (H2142) is negated and gives the ground of the charge: kindness was not remembered, and the needy were pursued instead.
In Psa 71:11 and Hos 8:3 forsaking or spurning (H5800A, H2186A) comes before the pursuit: the foes say God has forsaken him, and Israel has spurned the good, so the enemy pursues.
In Jos 8:24 'finished' (H3615G) marks the end of the killing in the field where Ai's men were pursued, before Israel returned to the city.
In Job 19:22 'satisfied' (H7646) is negated: the friends who pursue Job are not satisfied with his flesh.
In Nah 1:8 'complete' (H3617) is the end God makes of his adversaries, beside pursuing his enemies into darkness.
In 1Ti 6:11 'godliness' (eusebeia, G2150) is the second of the goods named as objects of pursue.
In Deu 19:6 'deserve' (mishpat, H4941G) is negated: the manslayer pursued by the avenger did not deserve to die.
In 2Sa 20:6 'fortified' (H1219) names the cities Sheba might reach, the reason David gives for pursuing him at once.
In Judg 20:45 'hard' (achar, H0310A) is the word after the verb that the ESV renders as the closeness of the pursuit: they were followed hard to Gidom.
In Exo 14:4 and Exo 14:8 'harden' (chazaq, H2388G) is the Lord's act on Pharaoh's heart, and the pursuit of Israel follows it.
In 1Sa 23:25 'heard' (H8085G) comes before the pursuit: Saul heard where David was and pursued him into the wilderness of Maon.
In Isa 51:1 'listen' (H8085G) is the call to those who pursue righteousness, opening the verse.
In Exo 14:4 and Exo 14:8 'heart' (lev, H3820A) is Pharaoh's, the object of the Lord's hardening that comes before the pursuit.
In 2Ti 2:22 'heart' (kardia, G2588) is the pure heart of those in whose company righteousness is pursued.
In Job 30:15 'honor' (H5082) is what is chased off as by the wind, the object of the verb the ESV turns into a passive, beside prosperity passed like a cloud.

In Jos 8:24, Judg 7:25 and Lam 3:43 killing (harag, H2026) goes with the pursuit: the men of Ai killed where they were pursued, Oreb and Zeeb killed before the pursuit of Midian, and Zion pursued and killed without pity.
In Exo 14:4 'know' (H3045) gives the purpose of the pursuit God brings about: the Egyptians shall know that he is the Lord.
In Jos 2:5 'know' (H3045) is negated in Rahab's word that she does not know where the men went, before she tells the king's men to pursue.
In 1Sa 25:29 'living' and 'lives' (H2416A, H5315H) set the life of the one pursued, bound in the bundle of the living with the Lord, against those who rise to pursue it.
In 1Sa 24:14 and Psa 143:3 'dead' (H4191) is a likeness: David names himself a dead dog that Saul pursues, and the pursued speaker is made to sit like those long dead.
In Num 14:45, 1Sa 23:25, 2Ch 14:13 and Eze 35:6 the words of living (H3427, H4241 with H0369, H2416A) give the place of those pursued, the end of the pursued, and God's oath 'as I live'.
In Deu 19:6 and Eze 35:6 'hated' (H8130) gives the legal ground: the manslayer had not hated his neighbor, and Edom did not hate bloodshed, so blood pursues.
In Hos 2:7 'lovers' (H0157G) are the object of the wife's pursuit, which does not reach them.
In 1Cor 14:1, 1Ti 6:11 and 2Ti 2:22 'love' (agape, G0026) is an object of the command to pursue, first in 1Cor 14:1.
In 1Sa 30:8 'surely' (H5381, H5337, infinitive absolutes) doubles the verbs of the Lord's answer: the pursuit he commands will surely overtake and surely rescue.
In 1Ti 6:11 'steadfastness' (hupomone, G5281) is one of the goods named as objects of pursue.
In Psa 7:5 'glory' (kavod, H3519) is laid in the dust by the enemy who is invited to pursue and overtake the speaker's soul.
In Jer 48:2 'silence' (H1826H) is what Madmen will be brought to, beside the sword that will pursue it.

In Jos 2:5, Jos 2:7, Jos 8:17 and Jos 8:24 the gate shut or the city left open (H5462, H6605A) and the open field (H7704G) set the place of the pursuit: the gate shut behind the pursuers, Ai left open, the men killed in the open.
In 1Sa 17:52 'wounded' (H2491A) names the Philistines who fell on the way as the men of Israel pursued them.
In Psa 109:16 'brokenhearted' (H3512A with levav, H3824) names the third group pursued to death, beside the poor and needy.
In Eze 35:6 'declares' (H5002) marks the sentence that blood shall pursue Edom as the Lord's own word.
In 1Cor 14:1 'prophesy' (G4395) is named as the gift to be desired most, after the command to pursue love.
In 1Sa 30:8 'answered' (H0559) introduces the Lord's reply to David's question whether to pursue.
In 2Sa 24:13 'answer' (H1697H) is what Gad must bring back after David chooses among the judgments, one of them a pursuit by foes.
In Psa 34:14, Rom 14:19, 2Ti 2:22 and 1Pe 3:11 'peace' (H7965G, G1515) is an object of the pursuit, in Psa 34:14 and 1Pe 3:11 first sought and then pursued.
In Amo 1:11 'cast off' (H7843) has pity as its object: Edom pursued his brother and cast off pity.
In Deu 28:45 'keep' (H8104G) belongs to the commandments not kept, the reason the curses pursue.
In Amo 1:11 'kept' (H8104G) has wrath as its object: Edom kept his wrath forever, beside the pursuit of his brother.
In Jer 48:2 'renown' (H8416) of Moab is no more, at the opening of the oracle in which the sword will pursue Madmen.
In Jos 8:24 'returned' (H7725G with H5704) closes the pursuit: when the killing in the open was finished, all Israel returned to Ai.
In 2Sa 24:13 'return' (H7725G with H4100) is the answer Gad must take back after David chooses among the judgments.
In Hos 2:7 'return' (H7725G) follows the failed pursuit: the wife resolves to go back to her first husband.
In Amo 1:11 and Jude 7 'punishment' (H5921A, G1349) follows the pursuit: for Edom it will not be revoked, and for the cities it is eternal fire.
In Job 30:15 'prosperity' (H3444) has passed away like a cloud, beside Job's honor pursued as by the wind.
In Psa 109:16 'poor' and 'needy' (H6041, H0034 with H0376I) name those pursued to be put to death.

In Isa 51:1, Rom 9:30, Rom 9:31, 1Ti 6:11 and 2Ti 2:22 'righteousness' (H6664G, G1343) is the object of the pursuit; in Rom 9:30 it is reached without pursuit and in Rom 9:31 the law of it pursued and not reached.
In Jude 7 'sexual immorality' (G1608) is what the cities indulged in, together with going after unnatural desire.
In Psa 71:11 'deliver' (H5337) is negated in the foes' words: there is none to deliver him, so they urge pursuit.
In 1Sa 23:25, 1Sa 25:29 and Hos 2:7 seeking (baqash, H1245) goes with the pursuit of a person: Saul seeks David, men seek David's life, the wife seeks her lovers and does not find them.
In Psa 34:14, 1Pe 3:11 and Isa 51:1 seeking (H1245, G2212) is paired with pursuing a good: peace sought and pursued, and those who pursue righteousness called those who seek the Lord.
In 2Sa 2:28 'stopped' (H5975G) ends the pursuit at Joab's trumpet.
In Psa 34:14 and 1Pe 3:11 doing good (H6213A, G4160G) stands between turning from evil and seeking and pursuing peace.
In Jude 7 'serve' (G4295) has the cities as subject: they serve as an example by their punishment.
In Jos 10:19 'given' (H5414G with H3588A) gives the ground of the command to pursue: the Lord has given the enemies into their hand.
In 2Ch 14:13 'broken' (H7665) names the Ethiopians as broken before the Lord and his army as Asa pursued them.
In Amo 1:11 'transgressions' (H6588) frame the charge against Edom, of which the pursuit of his brother is the one named.

In Gen 31:23, Judg 1:6, 2Sa 20:6, 2Ch 13:19, Psa 71:11 and Jer 39:5 taking or seizing (H3947G, H0270, H3920, H8610) is what the pursuit is for or ends in: kinsmen taken along, Adoni-bezek caught, cities taken, the one forsaken to be seized, Zedekiah taken.
In 2Sa 2:19, 2Sa 22:38 and Psa 18:37 turning (H5186, H7725G) is negated: the pursuer does not turn aside or back until the pursued is reached or consumed.
In Judg 20:45 'turned' (H6437G) is the flight of the pursued toward the wilderness, and in Job 30:15 'turned' (H2015) the terrors turned on Job.
In 2Sa 20:10 'observe' (H8104I) is negated: Amasa did not watch the sword in Joab's hand, before Joab and Abishai pursued Sheba.
In 1Sa 17:52 'shout' (H7321) goes with the rising of Israel and Judah before they pursued the Philistines.
In 2Sa 24:13 'consider' (H3045) is Gad's call to David to weigh the three judgments, one of them a pursuit by foes.

may_rest_on_besides.text: In Jude 7 aperchomai, usually to go away or depart (aorist participle), is rendered 'pursued' with 'unnatural desire' as its object: the cities went off after other flesh, so the going away is a going after a desire.
In Rom 9:31 dioko (pursue; present participle) has as object a law leading to righteousness, and the verse says Israel did not reach that law: a pursuit toward a goal that is not attained.
In Rev 12:13 dioko (aorist indicative) is the dragon's chase of the woman who bore the male child, after he was thrown down: a hostile pursuit of a person, not of a goal.

In Exo 14:8, Jos 8:16, Judg 4:16, 2Sa 2:19 and the other verses of this row, achar (after, behind; a preposition in construct) is the word after the verb of chasing that the ESV folds into 'pursued': it marks the one chased as ahead, and is not the act itself.
In Judg 20:45 dabaq, whose sense is to cling or keep close, is a Hiphil rendered 'pursued hard': those who fled were followed close and overtaken, and two thousand of them struck down.

In Num 14:45 katat, whose sense is to beat or crush, is a Hiphil the ESV renders 'pursued': the Amalekites and Canaanites beat Israel down and drove them as far as Hormah; the English hides the crushing.

In Gen 14:15, Exo 14:9, Jos 8:16, Judg 4:16, 1Sa 17:52, 2Sa 2:19, 2Ki 25:5, Psa 18:37 and the other verses of this reading, radaph (pursue; mostly Qal narrative) is chasing a fleeing person or army to overtake, capture or strike it, often with how far the chase ran.

In Psa 109:16, Psa 143:3, Amo 1:11 and Lam 3:43 radaph is pursuit of the weak to destroy them: the poor and needy to death, the speaker's soul crushed, a brother with the sword with pity cast off, a people killed without pity in anger.

In Job 30:15 radaph (Qal imperfect, third feminine, active) is rendered by the ESV as a passive, 'my honor is pursued': Job's honor is what is chased off as by the wind, beside terrors turned on him and prosperity passed like a cloud.
In 1Ti 6:11 de (but) is the particle the surface 'Pursue' carries with dioko at the same place: it opens the turn from fleeing these things to pursuing righteousness, and is not itself the act.

In Rom 14:19, 1Cor 14:1, 1Ti 6:11, 2Ti 2:22 and 1Pe 3:11 dioko (pursue; imperative or hortatory) has a good to be pursued as object: peace and mutual upbuilding, love, righteousness and the virtues listed, peace sought and pursued.
In Rom 9:30 dioko (present participle) is negated: the nations that made no pursuit of righteousness are said to have reached it, a righteousness by faith, so the reaching comes without the pursuit.

In Gen 35:5, Exo 14:4, Deu 19:6, Jos 10:19, 2Sa 17:1, Jer 48:2 and the other verses of this row, achar (after; a preposition in construct) stands with the verb of chasing that the ESV renders 'pursue', marking the one chased as ahead; it is not the act itself.
In Jer 48:2 halak (go, walk; Qal imperfect, feminine) with achar is rendered 'pursue' and has the sword as its subject: the sword will go after Madmen, a going that is a pursuit to destroy.

In Exo 14:4, Jos 2:5, Jos 10:19, 1Sa 30:8, 2Sa 20:6, Hos 8:3 and the other verses of this reading, radaph is chasing a person or a band to overtake or strike them: foretold, commanded, asked about, or negated as in Gen 35:5, where terror from God stops it.
In Exo 15:9 and Deu 19:6 the verse names what drives the pursuit: in Exo 15:9 the enemy's desire to have its fill of them, in Deu 19:6 the hot anger of the avenger of blood.

In 1Sa 25:29, Psa 7:5, Psa 71:11, Job 19:22 and Job 19:28 radaph is pursuit aimed at a person's life or standing: men seeking David's life, an enemy after the speaker's soul, foes saying God has forsaken him, Job's friends hounding him.

In Psa 83:15, Jer 29:18, Lam 3:66, Nah 1:8 and Job 13:25 God is the one who pursues: with tempest, with sword, famine and pestilence, in anger, into darkness, and in Job's question whether he will pursue dry chaff.
In Deu 28:22, Deu 28:45 and Eze 35:6 the pursuers are not persons: diseases and blight, the curses for disobedience, and blood for one who did not hate bloodshed pursue and overtake.
In Psa 34:14 and Isa 51:1 radaph has a good as its object: peace to be sought and pursued, and righteousness pursued by those who seek the Lord.
In Hos 2:7 radaph (Piel) is the unfaithful wife's chase of her lovers, which fails: she will not overtake them or find them, and then turns back to her first husband.

verses.text: Pursue love, and earnestly desire the spiritual gifts, especially that you may prophesy.
And each struck down his man. The Syrians fled, and Israel pursued them, but Ben-hadad king of Syria escaped on a horse with horsemen.
let him turn away from evil and do good; let him seek peace and pursue it.

And the men of Israel and Judah rose with a shout and pursued the Philistines as far as Gath and the gates of Ekron, so that the wounded Philistines fell on the way from Shaaraim as far as Gath and Ekron.
And Saul and his men went to seek him. And David was told, so he went down to the rock and lived in the wilderness of Maon. And when Saul heard that, he pursued after David in the wilderness of Maon.
After whom has the king of Israel come out? After whom do you pursue? After a dead dog! After a flea!

If men rise up to pursue you and to seek your life, the life of my lord shall be bound in the bundle of the living in the care of the Lord your God. And the lives of your enemies he shall sling out as from the hollow of a sling.

findings.text: In the battle and flight narratives (Gen 14:15, Exo 14:9, Judg 4:16, 1Sa 23:25, 2Sa 2:19, 2Ki 9:27, Jer 39:5 and the rest) one person or force runs after another who flees, to overtake, capture or strike them.
In Exo 15:9, Deu 19:6, 1Sa 25:29, Psa 7:5, Psa 109:16, Psa 143:3, Amo 1:11, Lam 3:43 and Rev 12:13 the pursuit is aimed at a person's life or at the weak, to destroy them.

parts.grounds: pursued the poor and needy and the brokenhearted

findings.text: The verses name what drives the pursuit: the enemy's desire to have its fill (Exo 15:9), the avenger's hot anger (Deu 19:6), Edom's anger and wrath kept forever (Amo 1:11), and God's anger in Lam 3:43 and Lam 3:66.

parts.grounds: my desire shall have its fill of them

findings.text: The hostile pursuit is carried on without turning back and without pity: kindness not remembered (Psa 109:16), killing without pity (Lam 3:43), pity cast off (Amo 1:11), no turning back till they were consumed (Psa 18:37, 2Sa 22:38).
What the pursuit issues in is named: taking and seizing (Gen 31:23, Judg 1:6, Jer 39:5), killing (Jos 8:24, Lam 3:43), destroying and consuming (Exo 15:9, Psa 18:37), death (Deu 19:6, Psa 109:16).
The pursuit is stopped or not begun in Gen 35:5, where terror from God falls on the cities, and in 2Sa 2:28, where Joab's trumpet ends the pursuit and the fighting.

parts.grounds: all the men stopped and pursued Israel no more

findings.text: In Psa 83:15, Jer 29:18, Lam 3:66, Nah 1:8 and Eze 35:6 God is the pursuer, with tempest, sword, anger or blood, toward a people or his enemies.

parts.grounds: You will pursue them in anger

findings.text: In Exo 14:4 and Exo 14:8 the Lord hardens Pharaoh's heart and Pharaoh pursues Israel, so that the Egyptians shall know that he is the Lord.

parts.grounds: the Lord hardened the heart of Pharaoh

findings.text: In Rom 14:19, 1Cor 14:1, 1Ti 6:11, 2Ti 2:22, 1Pe 3:11, Psa 34:14 and Isa 51:1 the hearers are called to pursue a good: peace, love, righteousness, faith, godliness, steadfastness and gentleness.

parts.grounds: let us pursue what makes for peace

findings.text: The pursuit of a good comes after a turning or a flight: turn from evil and do good, then seek peace and pursue it (Psa 34:14, 1Pe 3:11); flee these things or youthful passions, then pursue righteousness (1Ti 6:11, 2Ti 2:22).

parts.grounds: flee youthful passions and pursue righteousness

findings.text: In Rom 9:30 and Rom 9:31 pursuit and attainment part: the nations that did not pursue righteousness reached it by faith, and Israel that pursued a law leading to it did not reach it.

parts.grounds: a righteousness that is by faith

findings.text: In Jude 7 and Hos 2:7 the going after is of a forbidden desire: other flesh, and lovers the wife does not overtake or find.

parts.grounds: She shall pursue her lovers but not overtake them

findings.text: In Hos 2:7 the failed pursuit of the lovers is followed by a turning back: the wife resolves to return to her first husband, for it was better then.

parts.grounds: I will go and return to my first husband

findings.text: In the chase narratives the pursued flee or escape, the other half of the pursuit (Judg 1:6, Judg 8:12, 1Ki 20:20, 2Ki 9:27), and in 2Sa 24:13 fleeing before pursuing foes is one of three judgments.

parts.grounds: Adoni-bezek fled, but they pursued him

findings.text: In Job 30:15 Job's honor is chased off as by the wind while terrors are turned on him and his prosperity passes like a cloud.
Before the pursuit David inquires of the Lord and is told to pursue with the promise that he will surely overtake (1Sa 30:8); in Jos 8:16 and Judg 7:23 the people are first called together.

parts.grounds: Shall I pursue after this band

findings.text: The pursuit follows a forsaking: foes pursue the one they say God has forsaken and none will deliver (Psa 71:11), and the enemy pursues Israel that has spurned the good (Hos 8:3).

parts.grounds: God has forsaken him; pursue and seize him

findings.text: In Deu 19:6 and Eze 35:6 hatred is the legal ground: the manslayer pursued had not hated his neighbor and did not deserve to die, and blood pursues Edom because it did not hate bloodshed.

parts.grounds: since he had not hated his neighbor
